The big idea

Guiding questions

What structure do learned representations have,
how can we know,
and what follows from apparent agreement across models or modalities?

  • What structure? — geometry: similarity, neighbourhoods, directions, features
  • How can we know? — measurement: metrics, baselines, nulls, robustness
  • What follows? — interpretation: meaning, grounding, the limits of geometry

~1.5 min. The seminar is organised around this question, not around a catalogue of techniques. Every meeting contributes to one of the three parts.

The running case: Platonic Representation Hypothesis

The claim (Huh et al., 2024):
capable models converge toward a shared statistical model of reality.

The evidence:
alignment scores between models grow with model capability.

The critique (2026):
after calibration against proper null baselines, the global trend largely disappears.
One line of work finds only narrower local-neighbourhood agreement robust.
Another finds that this local agreement falls sharply as the evaluation gallery grows.

Our job:
learn enough geometry, statistics and network internals to adjudicate this dispute ourselves.

~2 min. This is live research, with load-bearing 2026 preprints. The point is not to arrive at “true” or “false”, but at the conclusion the evidence actually warrants.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain how training objectives shape an embedding space
  • Read an alignment claim critically:
    which metric? which comparison? which null? what is the warranted conclusion?
  • Weigh competing accounts of internal structure:
    superposition, sparse features, nonlinear features
  • Separate empirical claims about similarity
    from philosophical claims about meaning and grounding
  • Write a concise, evidence-based argument about current research

~1 min. A condensed version of the seven learning objectives in the announcement. The last one is what the final essays test.

This seminar …

… is a reading seminar:
short, bounded common readings for everyone
discussion that starts from shared evidence

… is not
a survey of representation learning
a coding course
a course in differential geometry or information theory

Workload: 3–4 hours of focused critical reading per week
Meetings 7 and 8 (just before Christmas) are the heaviest weeks

~1 min. Reading loads are calibrated in effective page equivalents; the schedule gives exact sections and page counts. “Bounded” means: read what is assigned, not the whole paper.

How the semester is built

Five stages

Meetings Stage
1–2 Concrete representations; why learning creates structure
3 The Platonic Representation Hypothesis: claim and evidence
4–5 The instrument (RSA, CKA) and its calibration
6–8 Test cases: multimodal alignment, superposition, sparse autoencoders
9–10 Meaning and grounding; debiasing and the alignment hypothesis
11 Supervised final essays

~1.5 min. PRH comes early (Meeting 3) so that the technical sessions have a purpose; the measurement sessions come right after, so the hypothesis is examined with the right tools.

Before Meeting 1: Session Zero

A mandatory, asynchronous on-ramp — to be completed before 28 Oct.

  • Refreshes what the readings assume:
    vectors, cosine similarity, PCA, embeddings, attention, residual stream
  • How to read a paper (Keshav): in several passes, not front to back
  • Optional: how to read with an AI chatbot — as a tutor, not a summariser
  • Pick only what you need; nobody is expected to work through everything

Course handouts: representation-comparison primer, concept glossary

~1 min. Session Zero exists so that regular meetings don’t turn into remedial lectures. Differential geometry and information theory are not prerequisites.

What you do each week

The weekly rhythm

  1. Read the required common readings (schedule has exact mandatory sections/parts)
  2. Write handwritten notes — on paper or a tablet with a digital pen
  3. Upload them as a (scanned) PDF to Moodle,
    every Wednesday before 16:00
  4. Discuss in the meeting

Your notes should contain:

  • notes on all required readings
  • the central claim and the evidence the authors offer for it, in your own words
  • connections to earlier readings, objections, or points of confusion
  • at least one concrete question for discussion

~1.5 min. No page minimum. Assessed for substantive engagement, not for handwriting, length, or agreement with the paper.

Why handwritten?

Your notes are your only aid in the final essay session.

The notes you submitted on Moodle are printed out
and handed to you there.

So: write the notes you will want to have on 27 Jan:
claims, evidence, limits — not a copy of the abstract.

Notes are notes on the readings,
not prepared essay answers — (will be blacked out on printouts).

~1 min. This is the central design decision: weekly preparation and the final assessment are the same body of work.

Notes on empirical papers

For the empirical readings (Meetings 3–6 and 10),
we recommend organising your notes around these questions:

  • What is the claim?
  • At which representation level?
  • Which metric or objective?
  • Compared to what?
  • What could confound it?
  • Which adjustments or robustness checks?
  • What is the result?
  • Warranted conclusion?

Last point is crucial: what does the evidence actually show?

Everyone reads the same papers every week.  Only in Meeting 6, two branch groups each add one reading with a different focus and report it to the class along these questions (groups assigned at least one week before).

~1 min. Previewed in the primer. It is a thinking tool for notes and discussion, not a form to fill in mechanically.

Discussion

Everyone contributes, and any substantive contribution counts:

  • precise, relevant questions
  • concise synthesis or summaries of earlier points
  • answers that are evidence-based / grounded in the readings
  • facilitating the discussion (clarifications, checking understanding, keeping disputes on track)

Good questions count as much as good arguments.

Attendance is mandatory at every meeting.

~30 s. You don’t need to have understood everything to contribute; saying precisely what you didn’t understand is a contribution.

Essays and grading

Practice essay over Christmas

When What
16 Dec Four prompts on Meetings 1–8
by 6 Jan Write one essay: by hand, ~45 min, only your submitted notes
Upload the scan, without your name
7–13 Jan Review one other essay, anonymously, in a Moodle form
13–20 Jan Instructors check each review, add their own
20 Jan Debrief at the end of Meeting 10

The essay is not marked.
A careful review earns up to 2 bonus points — if you submitted an essay yourself.

~2 min. Why: everyone gets individual feedback on a full essay a week before the final session, and reviewing someone else’s essay is the best way to learn the marking criteria. Nobody checks the 45 minutes — you only cheat yourself out of the rehearsal. Only essays submitted by 6 Jan take part in the review round.

Meeting 11: supervised final essays

  • Three hours, 27 Jan (time to be announced)
  • Six prompts; you answer two of your choice
  • Only aid: printouts of your own submitted notes

Marked out of 10 each, for:
conceptual accuracy
use of evidence and methodological reasoning
integration across meetings
clarity of argument

A Strong Essay

  • defines the claim it is about
  • distinguishes it from nearby claims
  • uses specific evidence from the readings
  • explains at least one methodological limitation
  • reaches a proportionate conclusion

A list of paper summaries is not an argument.

~1.5 min for both slides. This is the final-essay checklist from the schedule; the practice essay and the peer review use the same criteria.

Grading: 40 points, plus up to 2 bonus

Points
Notes: 1 point per regular meeting 10
Discussion: 1 point per regular meeting 10
Two final essays, 10 each 20
Bonus: peer review of a practice essay max. +2
  • One free pass for missing notes;
    further missing notes count only with a doctor’s note
  • Attendance is mandatory:
    two unexcused absences mean failing the seminar

~1 min. “Sensible notes” is a yes/no call, not a fine-grained mark.
